analysis.one_liner: Bans new federal leases for coal, oil, and gas on public lands and offshore waters.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Energy Committee; it died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the federal government from selling any new leases to extract coal, oil, tar sands, oil shale, or gas from federal land, and from issuing new offshore drilling leases in the Arctic, Atlantic, Pacific, or Gulf of Mexico. It would also have canceled existing offshore leases in the Beaufort Sea, Cook Inlet, and Chukchi Sea. Its stated purpose was to keep most federal fossil fuels unburned so the U.S. could avoid the worst effects of climate change and speed the shift to clean energy. It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and was never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who bear the costs of climate change — stronger storms, wildfires, droughts, and rising seas — and communities near federal coal and oil development that face pollution. The bill's own findings say ending new federal leases would prevent roughly 90 percent of the potential emissions from federal fossil fuels.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone exposed to climate change effects

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares it U.S. policy to manage federal land and waters to avoid the most dangerous impacts of climate change and to promote a rapid transition to a clean energy economy. [S2]
It would prohibit any new lease, renewal, or extension for coal, oil, tar sands, oil shale, or gas on federal land subject to the Mineral Leasing Act. [S2][S3]

It would bar the Interior Department from issuing any new offshore drilling lease or authorization in the Arctic Ocean, Atlantic Ocean, Pacific Ocean, Gulf of Mexico, or any other part of the outer Continental Shelf. [S2][S3]
Within 60 days of enactment, Interior would have to cancel existing offshore leases in the Beaufort Sea, Cook Inlet, and Chukchi Sea. [S2][S3]

The bill's findings cite research that keeping warming under 2 degrees Celsius requires leaving at least 80 percent of proven fossil fuel reserves unburned, and that ending new federal leases would prevent 90 percent of potential emissions from federal fossil fuels. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel companies that extract coal, oil, and gas from federal land and offshore waters would lose access to new federal leases and, in the Arctic seas, existing leases. Some energy consumers and coal-dependent local governments could face higher fuel prices and lost royalty revenue over time.

drawbacks.text: The bill stops new federal fossil fuel supply without any paired plan for workers, communities, or state budgets that currently depend on coal and oil royalties, so the transition costs would fall on specific places even as the climate benefit is shared broadly. [S2][S3]

Because the U.S. would still consume fossil fuels, cutting federal supply could shift some production to private or foreign sources, reducing the climate benefit while raising costs for American buyers — the standard objection to supply-side restrictions. [S3]

Canceling existing Arctic leases would likely trigger lawsuits and compensation claims from leaseholders, which is why the bill includes an exception allowing renewals where a court would likely find a material breach of contract. [S2][S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The climate case is large: federal fossil fuels account for a significant share of the U.S. emissions budget, and the bill would prevent most of those potential emissions. But the bill is a blunt instrument — it cuts supply with no transition assistance for coal communities and no direct limits on demand, so some extraction would likely shift elsewhere and prices could rise. An honest supporter would acknowledge those gaps; an honest opponent would acknowledge the climate stakes the bill addresses are real.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 2015 and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Keep It in the Ground Act of 2015 on November 4, 2015, joined by original cosponsors including Sens. Sanders, Boxer, Gillibrand, Leahy, Cardin, and Warren. [S1][S3]
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day. [S1][S5]
The bill received 8 cosponsors — 7 Democrats and 1 Independent — over its lifetime. [S4]
No further action was recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and gas companies that lease federal land and offshore waters are better off: no new leases were blocked and no existing Arctic leases were canceled, so extraction on federal territory continued under the pre-existing rules.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. Sanders, Boxer, Gillibrand, Leahy, Cardin, and Warren
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 8 cosponsors (7 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill during the 114th Congress.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Lisa Murkowski
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration, keeping it from any committee or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 supporters were Democrats or the Independent who caucuses with Democrats, and the Republican-run Energy Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill ends all new coal leases on federal land, which is where a large share of U.S. coal is mined. Blocking those leases would cut off the cheapest long-term supply of coal for leaseholders.
No new leases anywhere on the outer Continental Shelf, and existing leases in the Beaufort Sea, Cook Inlet, and Chukchi Sea would be canceled outright.

industries.industry: Onshore oil, gas, tar sands, and oil shale producers
industries.note: The bill bars new lease sales, renewals, and extensions for all onshore federal fossil fuels under the Mineral Leasing Act, though national-security and contract-breach exceptions allow narrow carve-outs.
